6.238.m: Rudra said: / Knowing his brother to be slain, Hiraṇyakaśipu then, / that great Daitya, performed austerity on the slope of Meru directed toward me.
For thousands of divine years, subsisting on wind, endowed with great strength, / chanting the five-syllable mantra, he worshiped me, O auspicious one.
Then with a delighted mind I said to that great Asura: / 'Choose a boon, O Daiteya, whatever is in your mind.' / Then the Daiteya spoke to me, who was pleased, O fair-faced one:
Hiraṇyakaśipu said: / [To be incapable of being slain] by gods, Asuras, humans, Gandharvas, serpents, and Rākṣasas, / and by beasts, birds, wild animals, and the great-souled Siddhas,
by Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, and Kinnaras as well, / by any of the diseases, and likewise by weapons, / and by all the foremost sages: grant me invulnerability!

Rudra said:
“So be it!”—thus, O lovely-faced one, I spoke to that demon. / Having obtained a great boon from me, that mighty son of Diti,
having conquered Mahendra and the gods, became the lord of the three worlds, / and by force seized all sacrificial portions for himself.
Vanquished by him, the gods found no protector. / The Gandharvas, gods, and Dānavas were all his servants;
the Yakṣas, Nāgas, Siddhas, and Sādhyas were obedient to his will. / The daughter of Uttānapāda, a girl named Kalyāṇī,
The mighty king of the Daityas married according to the prescribed rite. / From her was born, O auspicious lady, the glorious Prahlāda, the king of Daityas.
who was devoted to Hṛṣīkeśa, Hari, even while dwelling in the womb, / [devoted] in all states and actions, through mind, speech, and bodily deeds.
With a serene mind, he knew no other than the eternal Lord of gods. / In due time, modest and intelligent, he resided in his teacher's house,
having studied all the Vedas and diverse sacred scriptures. / Then, after some time, the son of the Daitya, accompanied by his teacher,
approached his father and bowed with humility. / Embracing his son endowed with auspicious marks with both arms, / placing him on his lap, the lord of the Daityas, greatly astonished, said this:
Hiraṇyakaśipu said: / "Prahlāda, you have dwelt for a long time in the house of the guru. / O you of good vows, tell me that knowledge which was spoken by the guru."
Rudra said: / Thus questioned by his own father, Prahlāda, a Vaiṣṇava from birth, / spoke with love to the lord of Daityas words that remove defilement.
Prahlāda said: / "Having bowed to that all-pervading Viṣṇu, / who indeed is the meaning of all the Upaniṣads, the Puruṣa, the Lord, I shall speak to you."

Rudra said:
Hearing this praise of Viṣṇu, the king of the Daityas was filled with astonishment. / In anger he said to the teacher: “What have you taught my son?
O evil-minded one, why have you taught my son such praise of Hari, / an act of foolishness, an improper deed unworthy of a brāhmaṇa?
This unmentionable praise of my enemy has been uttered before me / even by a child, surely by your favor, O lowest of the twice-born!”
Having said this, looking around, the king of Daityas, overcome with anger, / said to one Daitya: "Bind this vile twice-born!"
Hearing the king's words, he bound the son of Bhṛgu. / Seeing his guru being bound, Prahlāda, who was dear to brāhmaṇas, / said to his father: "Father, this was not told to me by the guru."
By the grace of the God of gods, Hari, I have been instructed, O lord. / I have no other teacher; it is Hari alone who prompts me.

He is the hearer, thinker, speaker, seer, the all-pervading Lord. / Hari alone is the imperishable creator and controller of all embodied beings. / Therefore this sinless brāhmaṇa teacher must be released, O lord!”

Rudra said:
Hearing his son's words, Hiraṇyakaśipu then / released that brāhmaṇa and said to his own son in astonishment:
“Why, child, are you deluded in this way by the false words of a twice-born? / Who is Viṣṇu? What is his form? Where does that Hari reside?
I alone am the Lord in the world, since I am the master of the three worlds. / Worship me alone; abandon Govinda, my unapproachable enemy!
Or else worship Lord Śaṅkara, Rudra, the teacher and master of the worlds, / Śiva, the presiding deity over the Asuras, who bestows all sovereignty.
Applying the tripuṇḍra with ashes, revered by the Daityas, / and worshiping Mahādeva according to the path declared in the Pāśupata scriptures!”

Rudra said:
Hearing the words of the lord of the Daityas, the priests of the Daityas [spoke].

The priests said:
“Just so, just so, O fortunate one! Obey the words of your father! / Abandon the enemy, the foe of Kaiṭabha, and worship the three-eyed Lord!
There is no god higher than Rudra, who bestows everything upon mortals. / Even your father became sovereign by his grace alone!”
Rudra said: / Hearing these words of theirs, Prahlāda, a Vaiṣṇava from birth—
Prahlāda said: / "Ah, supreme is the māyā of the Lord, by which the world is deluded! / Ah, those who know Vedānta are worshipped in all the worlds!"
even brāhmaṇas, out of recklessness, speak thus, filled with arrogance! / Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme truth.
Nārāyaṇa is the highest object of meditation; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditation. / He is the refuge of the whole universe, eternal, auspicious, and infallible.
Vāsudeva is the eternal creator and arranger of the universe. / The Puruṣa is indeed this universe; the universe subsists on him.
Having a golden form, eternal, with eyes resembling a lotus, / the gentle lord of Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā, stainless, of auspicious form.
By him alone were Brahmā and Īśa created at creation, the supreme and pervasive gods; / keeping his command foremost, Brahmā and Śaṅkara continue to exist.
From fear of him the wind blows; from fear the sun rises; / from fear of him fire and moon, and then death as the fifth, runs.
There was only Hari, the divine god, Nārāyaṇa, the supreme; / neither Brahmā, nor Indra, nor Īśāna, nor the moon and sun,
nor sky and earth, nor the lunar mansions, nor the gods. / The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus abandoning the meaning of all the Upaniṣads, O best of the twice-born, / why do you speak before me out of passion, greed, or fear?
Abandoning that god who protects all, Hari, the Lord of all, / how should I resort to heresy and worship Śaṅkara?
The husband of Lakṣmī, the God of gods, the infinite, the Supreme Person, / dark as the blue lotus petal, with eyes as broad as lotus leaves,
his chest marked by the Śrīvatsa, adorned with all ornaments, / ever youthful, the Lord of all, bestower of eternal bliss and joy,
Kṛṣṇa, upon whom the great-souled yogins like Sanaka and others meditate, / whom the hosts of gods headed by Brahmā, Īśa, and Śakra worship,
by half a glance from whose consort the celestials— / Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Varuṇa, Yama, Soma, and the lord of wealth—are looked upon,
by the mere remembrance of whose name swift liberation, / which is so difficult even for Brahmā and the others to attain, comes to living beings, even sinners.
He alone is the Lord of Śrī, always the protector even of the gods. / Him alone, Acyuta united with Lakṣmī, will I worship.
Most easily indeed will I attain that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.” / Rudra said: Hearing his words, Hiraṇyakaśipu then,
overtaken by fierce wrath, blazed like another fire. / Looking around at the Daityas, overcome with anger, he spoke:
Hiraṇyakaśipu said: / "By terrible arrays of weapons strike down, by my command, / the evil-doing Prahlāda, who is intent upon worshipping the enemy!"
‘Hari alone is the protector’—so let him be protected by him out of affection! / Today itself let me see his protection by Hari bear fruit!”

Rudra said:
Then the Daiteyas, with raised weapons, in order to kill the son of the Daitya lord, / stood surrounding that great-souled one by order of the Daitya sovereign.
Prahlāda too, having meditated on Viṣṇu in the lotus of his heart, / chanting the eight-syllable mantra, stood motionless like another mountain.
The warriors struck him all around with tridents, javelins, and spears. / There, O auspicious lady, Prahlāda's body, on account of remembering Hari,
By Viṣṇu's invincible power, [Prahrāda's body] became like an adamantine diamond. / Then, reaching his body, the great weapons of the gods' enemies,
fell broken to the ground like blue lotus petals, O fair one! / The Daityas were unable to pierce even the least part of his body.
The soldiers stood bewildered, hanging their heads before the Daitya king. / Seeing his son of such great stature and immense strength,
the king of the Daityas, filled with utter astonishment and overcome with fury, / then commanded all the highly poisonous serpents,
frightful ones headed by Vāsuki, in anger: "Devour him!" / Then, commanded by that king, those extremely powerful serpents,
with blazing mouths, terrible to behold, bit that exceedingly strong youth. / Having bitten that devotee of Garuḍadhvaja, those serpents whose weapons are venom,
The wind-eaters [serpents] became poisonless with shattered fangs, / their bodies torn by thousands of Garuḍas, extremely agitated.
they fled in all directions, profusely vomiting blood. / Seeing the great serpents in such a state, the Daitya lord then
angrily commanded the elephants of the quarters, full of rut. / Then, ordered by the king, the elephants of the quarters, maddened by rut,
surrounded him and struck him repeatedly with their massive tusks. / Thereupon the tusks of the quarter-elephants broke off at their roots and fell to the ground.
Deprived of their tusks, the elephants fled in terror. / Then, seeing those great elephants [flee], the powerful lord of the Daityas was enraged;
Having kindled a great fire, he threw in his own son. / Seeing Prahlāda, beloved of the one who reclines upon the waters, the carrier of oblations [fire]
did not burn the steadfast boy, and the flame became delightfully cool. / Seeing the child unburned, the king was utterly astonished.
Then he gave him terrible poison, [ordinarily harmful] to all living beings; / but through the power of Viṣṇu, that poison became nectar for him.
By offering it to that god, he consumed the poison as nectar. / Having thus tried to confound his son by these and other means of execution,
terrible and exceedingly cruel in form, and perceiving his invulnerability, / the Daitya king, overwhelmed with amazement, then addressed his son conciliatingly:
Hiraṇyakaśipu said: / "You have properly declared the supremacy of Viṣṇu before me. / Because he pervades all beings, he is called Viṣṇu.
The god who is all-pervading is indeed the Supreme Lord. / So show me his all-pervading nature visibly!
Sovereignty, power, splendor, knowledge, valor, and strength / are the supreme form, qualities, and divine glories of that highest one.
Only after having carefully seen him directly will I believe in Viṣṇu of the heaven-dwellers. / There is no one among the gods who matches my strength in the world.

By the boon granted by Īśāna, I have obtained invulnerability from all beings / and unconquerability by all beings, O honor-giver! / Viṣṇu may attain supremacy if he defeats me by his strength and valor!"
Rudra said: / Hearing his words, Prahlāda, astonished, spoke; / the one of good vows recounted the power of Hari to the Daitya.
Prahlāda said: / "He who is that glorious Nārāyaṇa, the eternal supreme Self, / because of his dwelling in all beings, is called Vāsudeva."
He is called Viṣṇu as the creator of the entire world. / Indeed, there is nothing other than him in this universe of the moving and unmoving.

Everywhere, the form of conscious and unconscious matter belongs only to him; it is not otherwise. / Three quarters of his pervade the supreme heaven, while a single quarter's wondrous expansion [is this world].
Janārdana, who holds the discus and mace in his hands and is clad in yellow robes, / is perceived by yogins through devotion; without devotion, he is never perceived anywhere.
Janārdana cannot be perceived through anger or envy. / In gods, animals, and men, and among unmoving beings, / he abides, pervading all, both the lowly and the great."
Rudra said: / Then, hearing Prahlāda's words, the best of Daityas, / with eyes red with fury, spoke, rebuking his son repeatedly.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said: / "If this Viṣṇu is indeed all-pervading and the Supreme Person, / then show me proof today! What is the use of speaking at such length?"
Mahādeva said: / Having spoken thus, the Daitya suddenly struck a pillar of his palace / with his hand and said this to Prahlāda:
Hiraṇyakaśipu said: / "Show that Viṣṇu in this [pillar], if he is all-pervading! / Otherwise, I will kill you, a babbler of falsehoods!"
Rudra said: / Having spoken thus, the lord of the sons of Diti suddenly drew his sword / and struck it at Prahlāda's chest, in fury wishing to slay him with the sword.
At that moment, a tremendous sound was heard loud within the pillar, / as if the intermediate space of the sky had split open with the roars of the thunderbolt of cosmic dissolution.
By that immense sound which deafened the ears of the Daityas, / all of them were knocked down to the earth like trees whose roots are severed.
Terrified, the Daityas thought the three worlds were inundated. / Then out of the pillar emerged the exceedingly glorious Great Hari.
He uttered a terrible roar like that of the destruction of the universe; / by that deafening roar, the stars fell to the earth.
Assuming a man-lion form, Hari manifested right there, / enveloped in the fiery brilliance of many tens of millions of suns.
His face resembled a lion's, while his body bore human form; / his face was terrifying with fangs, his flickering tongue lifted up to the sky,
the fringes of his mane surrounded by flames, his eyes resembling molten firebrands, the all-pervading Lord; / with a thousand long arms endowed with all kinds of weapons,
he shone like Mount Meru surrounded by trees with many branches; / wearing divine garlands and garments, adorned with celestial ornaments,
he stood in the form of a man-lion to destroy all the Dānavas. / Seeing that exceedingly powerful Narasiṃha of terrible aspect,
With his eyelashes burned, the lord of Daityas fell down, his limbs agitated. / Then Prahlāda, seeing Hari appearing as Nṛsiṃha,
Prahrāda paid homage to the Lord of Gods, Janārdana, with shouts of victory. / In the limbs of that great-souled Nṛsiṃha he saw
the worlds, the oceans with the continents, the gods, Gandharvas, and men; / and a thousand cosmic eggs were seen at the tips of his mane.
In his eyes the moon, sun, and other luminaries were seen; / in his ears the twin gods, the Aśvins, and the cardinal and intermediate directions;
upon his forehead Brahmā and Rudra; the sky and wind in his nostrils; / Indra and Agni at the edge of his mouth, and Sarasvatī on his tongue;
lions, tigers, śarabhas, and great serpents on his fangs; / and Meru was seen in his throat, and the great mountains on his shoulders;
gods, animals, and humans upon the arms of that great-souled one; / the atmosphere in his navel, and the earth in his feet;
all medicinal herbs in the pores of his body, trees in the rows of his nails, / and the Vedas with their auxiliary and secondary branches in his breaths;
the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts; / and the Gandharvas and Apsarases were seen in all his limbs.
In this way the manifestations of the Supreme Self were seen, / his chest adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and beautified by the garland of forest flowers,
endowed with weapons such as the conch, discus, mace, sword, and the Śārṅga bow; / having seen the meaning of all the Upaniṣads, the son of the Daitya king [bowed].
His limbs drenched with tears of joy, he bowed down again and again. / But the lord of Daityas, seeing Hari, fell under the sway of death through rage.
Lifting his sword to fight, he charged at that Nṛsiṃha. / Then all the Daitya hosts, regaining consciousness, possessed of immense strength,
seized their weapons and swiftly struck at Hari. / Just as stalks of straw thrown repeatedly into fire,
so indeed those great missiles turned to ashes upon Hari's body. / Seeing those armies of the Daityas, the Man-Lion then
burned them with his manes, clearly formed of wreaths of flames. / By the fire sprung from the manes of the Man-Lion, the Dānavas were utterly
All his hosts were reduced to ashes; that army was completely destroyed. / Leaving Prahlāda along with his followers, seeing that army reduced to ashes,
the lord of the Daityas, out of wrath, drew his sword and rushed forward. / But with one arm, the lord of gods seized the lord of Daityas, sword in hand,
and hurled him down just as a mighty wind fells a branch. / Grasping that huge-bodied one fallen upon the ground, the Man-Lion
placed him upon his lap; he looked at Hari's face. / The sin committed by reviling Viṣṇu, as well as that born from offenses against Vaiṣṇavas,
was then burned to ashes merely by the touch of Nṛsiṃha. / Then the Man-Lion, upon the great body of the lord of the Daityas,
tore it open with sharp, solid claws resembling thunderbolts. / With his soul purified, seeing the face of Hari directly before him,
his heart torn open by claws, having achieved his goal, he abandoned his life-breaths. / Rending that body into a hundred pieces with his sharp claws, the great Hari,
pulling out the long intestines, lovingly hung them around his neck. / Then all the hosts of gods and the ascetics rich in penance,
placing Brahmā and Rudra at their head, slowly approached to praise him. / Fearful, seeking to appease him who blazed with faces in every direction,
they meditated upon the Goddess, the mother and sustainer of the worlds, / golden-complexioned, yellow-robed, the destroyer of all distress.
Having meditated upon the auspicious Nārāyaṇī, Viṣṇu’s eternally faultless-limbed [consort], / they bowed with devotion to the eternal goddess through recitations of the Devīsūkta.
Meditated upon by them, that Goddess appeared right there at that moment: / four-armed, large-eyed, adorned with all ornaments,
clad in fine silk garments, with heavenly garlands and ointments. / Seeing her, the beloved of the God of gods, all the heaven-dwellers,
with folded hands, said to the Goddess: "Make your beloved propitious! / Act so that the Master may grant safety to the three worlds!"
Rudra said: / Thus addressed, the Goddess quickly went to her beloved Janārdana; / bowing down and paying homage, she said to him, "Be pleased!"
Seeing her, his own beloved queen, Hari, the Lord of all, / abandoned in an instant the wrath born of the demon’s body, like one filled with love.
Taking that Goddess upon his lap and embracing her, the treasury of mercy, / Hari looked upon the gods with a glance moist with the nectar of compassion.
Then, among those who were loudly praising him with "Victory, victory!" and bowing down, / and who were seen by his compassionate glance, there arose joyful excitement.
Then all the hosts of gods, their minds overflowing with joy, / with folded hands spoke to the Lord, bowing down to the protector of the universe.
The hosts of gods said: / "We are unable to behold your exceedingly wondrous splendor, O protector of the universe! / Wondrous indeed is this form of yours, marked with many arms and feet.
Pervading the three worlds, exceedingly fierce is your splendor; / all of us heaven-dwellers are unable to behold it or to stand before it."
Mahādeva said: / Thus implored by the gods, the lord of gods withdrew that / most terrifying splendor and became pleasant to behold.
Resembling ten million autumn moons, with eyes resembling lotuses, / with an auspicious mass of nectarous manes resembling ten million lightning flashes,
with divine armlets made of various gems and accompanied by bracelets, / with arms like the multitude of branches of the wish-fulfilling tree bearing good fruits,
endowed with four soft, divine arms, the Supreme Lord / was adorned with lotus hands resembling the hibiscus flower.
The Man-Lion shone with raised hands holding the conch and the discus, / and with the other two hands granting boons and freedom from fear,
his chest marked by the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha, adorned with the forest garland, / radiant with two earrings resembling rising suns,
amply adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and ornaments; / joined with Śrī situated on his left side, the Man-Lion shone resplendent.
Seeing that Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha, the deities along with the great sages, / sprinkled with tears of bliss, their hearts filled with joy,
immersed in an ocean of bliss, bowed down incessantly; / they worshipped the Lord of their souls by offering divine flowers.
Bathing the eternal one with jewel-pitchers filled with nectar, / with garments, ornaments, fragrant pastes, flowers, and charming incenses,
and worshipping the Man-Lion with heavenly lamps offered to him, / they praised him with divine hymns and bowed again and again.
Then, being pleased, the Lord of Lakṣmī granted their desired boons. / Then the Lord of all, affectionate toward his devotees, along with the hosts of gods,
He made Prahlāda the imperishable king of all the Daityas. / Having consoled his devotee Prahlāda, after consecrating him along with the foremost gods,
he granted him his desired boons and unswerving devotion. / Then, being praised by all the hosts of gods, the Man-Lion,
upon whose form flowers had been scattered, vanished right there. / Then all the hosts of gods went to their respective abodes,
and with delighted minds they once again enjoyed their sacrificial shares. / Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, became free from fear.
When that great Daitya was slain, all indeed rejoiced. / Then the Vaiṣṇava Prahlāda ruled the kingdom righteously.
Having obtained the kingdom by the grace of Hari, that best of Vaiṣṇavas, / worshipping the Man-Lion through numerous sacrifices, charitable gifts, and other rites,
In time he reached the eternal abode of Hari, accessible to yogins. / Those who always hear this deed of Prahlāda,

all of them, freed from sin, will attain the supreme state. / This majesty of Hari as Nṛsiṃha has been narrated to you, O goddess; / hear also about the remaining conditions of his majesty in proper order, O goddess.

6.239.m: Rudra said: / A son was born to Prahlāda, named Virocana. / His son was the long-armed, mighty Bali, [resplendent like] fire.
He was the foremost of those knowing dharma, true to his word, self-controlled, / the dearest devotee of Hari, ever devoted to dharma, and pure.
Having conquered all the gods, including Indra and the Marut hosts, / and having brought the three worlds under his control, that mighty one ruled the kingdom.
The earth ripened crops without cultivation, yielding abundant grains and fruits; / all cows yielded full milk; the trees were adorned with fruits and flowers.
Devoted to their own duty, all men were free from sin; / free from feverish grief, they constantly worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa.
Thus the mighty lord of the Daityas ruled his kingdom righteously; / the thirty gods, led by Indra, attended him as servants.
Having removed the pride of strength, he enjoyed sovereignty over the three worlds. / Seeing his son deprived of his kingdom, and desiring his welfare,
the righteous Kaśyapa, accompanied by his wife Aditi / and observing the milk-diet vow, performed austerity directed to Hari.
He worshipped the lord of gods, Padmanābha Janārdana. / For thousands of years Hari was worshipped by him;
right there the eternal one manifested himself to him along with the goddess. / Seeing him, the lotus-eyed, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
dark like a sapphire, adorned with all ornaments, / shining with a radiant crown, armlets, necklaces, and ear-rings,
with a chest illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, wrapped in a yellow garment, / seated with Śrī upon the great, supreme circle—
having seen that lord of the worlds with a heart filled with joy, / the best of the twice-born bowed down along with his wife and praised him:
Kaśyapa said: / Homage, homage to you, Lord of Lakṣmī, Omniscient One, Sovereign of the Universe, / Self of All, Lord of All Gods, cause of creation and destruction!
To the one without beginning or end, of infinite form, sustainer of the universe, / homage to you whose form is the Veda and its limbs, eye of all!
Homage to you, the Self of all, and homage to the subtlest of the subtle; / homage to the one filled with auspicious qualities, whose nature is meditated upon by yogins!
Homage to the youthful Kumāra, lord of Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā, / the sole enjoyment of the eternally liberated, abiding in the supreme abode!
Homage to you of fourfold self! Homage to you of fourfold emanation! / Homage to you in five states; homage to you who consist of fivefold nature!
You are worshipped always by yogins established in the fivefold essence, / residing in the five purificatory rites of those knowing the five realities.
Your other fivefold form is ever to be known, O Hari; / the wise surely know you as the perfect self in four ways.
Your servants purify the entire world, your creation; / the twice-born, filled with the three Vedas, dedicated to action, are dear to your devotees.
From their compassionate glance alone comes release from worldly bondage. / Homage to the supporter of the three worlds, self-sustainer, self of everything!
To the creator, the ordainer, the all, to you whose form is the cosmos, homage! / To Nārāyaṇa, to Kṛṣṇa, to Vāsudeva the bowman, / to Viṣṇu, to the victorious one, homage to you of pure sattva!
Mahādeva said: / Being thus duly praised with hymns by the great sage, / Janārdana, well-pleased, spoke with a deep voice.
The Blessed Lord said: / I am well-pleased, O best of the twice-born; you have worshipped me with devotion. / Choose a boon; may it be well with you; I shall grant your desire.
Mahādeva said: / Then Kaśyapa, accompanied by his wife, addressed Hṛṣīkeśa.
Kaśyapa said: / O Lord of Gods, becoming my son, bring welfare to the thirty gods! / O God, the three worlds have been conquered by Bali by force.
Becoming Indra’s younger brother, well-known as Upendra, / having conquered Bali by some means or through illusion, / give the three worlds perpetually to my son Śakra.
Mahādeva said: / Thus addressed by that brāhmaṇa, Janārdana said, 'So be it'; / and, praised by the thirty gods, he vanished right there.
At that very time, the Blessed Lord, the creator of beings, / entered the womb of Aditi [conceived] from the noble Kaśyapa.
At that time, Bali, of great ascetic power, began an extended sacrificial session / according to the rules, accompanied by eight great sages.

6.240.m: Śrī Mahādeva said: / Then, at the end of a thousand years, Aditi gave birth / to Vāmana, the unswerving Viṣṇu, the great lord of all worlds,
having the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha on his chest, with the brilliance of the full moon, / handsome, lotus-eyed, very short in body, Hari,
the god who assumed the form of a celibate student, the range of all the Veda's limbs, / the Lord marked with the signs of girdle, antelope-skin, staff, and the like.
Seeing him, all the deities, led by the god of a hundred sacrifices, / along with the great sages, praised him and bowed to the one of great splendour.
Then the gracious Lord spoke to the best of gods; / Vāmana said: 'What should be done by me today? Tell me that, O best of gods.'
Śrī Śaṃkara said: / Then, delighted, the thirty gods said to the supreme Lord; / the gods said: / 'At this time, O Madhusūdana, the sacrifice of Bali is taking place.
This is a time when that lord of the Daityas refuses nothing, O Lord; / having asked for the heavenly realm, you ought to give it to us.'
Śaṃkara said: / Having been thus addressed by all the thirty gods, Hari approached Bali, / who was seated at the sacrificial ground along with eight sages.
Seeing that guest arrive, the king of the Daityas rose up quickly; / Viṣṇu himself had arrived as a guest, endowed with legendary lore.
He worshipped him according to rule, having seated him on a seat of flowers, / and bowing and paying homage, he spoke in a faltering voice:
Bali said: / 'I am fortunate; I have achieved my goal; my life has borne fruit. / Having worshipped you, O lord of brāhmaṇas, what pleasure of yours may I accomplish?
Whatever purpose you have come for, directing yourself to me, O best of the twice-born, / that I shall grant you quickly; speak, O best among knowers of the Veda!'
Śaṃkara said: / Then with a delighted mind, he spoke to the king of the earth; / Vāmana said: 'Listen, O king of kings! I will state the reason for my coming.
Give me, O lord of the Daityas, land for a sacrificial fire-pit, / measuring three paces of my stride; I desire nothing else, O honor-giver.
Of all gifts, the gift of land is supreme; / whatever king gives land to an indigent brāhmaṇa,
even if it be only the size of a thumb, he becomes a lord of the earth; / there is nothing pure here like the gift of land.
He who accepts land and he who gives land, / both of them are performers of meritorious deeds, and at death go to heaven.

Therefore, O great king, give me three paces of land; / do not hesitate, O lord of the earth, to give such a small piece of land; / that gift of yours, O king, will become the giving of the three worlds.'
Śaṃkara said: / Then, with a joyful face, the lord of the earth said, 'So be it,' / and he resolved to make the gift of land to him according to rule.
Seeing that king of the Daityas, his household priest, / Uśanas indeed, spoke these words: 'Do not give the land, O king!'
Śukra said: / 'This is Viṣṇu, the supreme Lord, entreated by the gods, O king; / he has come here to deceive you and obtain the entire earth from you.
Therefore, land must not be given to that great-souled one, O king; / grant another wealth at my word, O ruler of the earth!'
Śrī Śaṃkara said: / Then, laughing, that king replied to his guru with firmness; / Bali said: 'For the pleasure of Vāsudeva, all merit has been performed by me.'
"Today I am blessed, if Viṣṇu himself has arrived. / Today life itself and supreme happiness ought to be given to him.

Therefore I shall bestow even the three worlds upon him without delay."
Śrī Śaṃkara said:
Having spoken thus, the king, washing his feet with devotion,
Gave the desired land preceded by pouring water according to the prescribed rite; / circumambulating him, bowing down, and giving wealth as a sacrificial fee,

He spoke again to that brahmin with a joyful inner self.
Bali said:
"I am blessed, I have achieved my purpose, having given you the earth, O twice-born one.

Take this earth as it pleases you, O chief of brahmins."
Śrī Śaṃkara said:
Viṣṇu said to that king: "O king, right beside you,

I shall measure the earth with a step today as you watch."
Having said this, abandoning that dwarfish form, the Supreme Lord,
Taking on the Trivikrama body, seized this earth, / fifty crores [of yojanas] wide, along with its oceans and mountains,
With its seas and islands, along with gods, asuras, and human beings. / With a single foot of his body, Madhusūdana traversed it;
The eternal one said to the lord of the Daityas: "What shall I do?" / That Trivikrama form of the Lord was indeed exceedingly majestic;
Even though it was for the benefit of the gods and the great-souled sages, / it could not even be seen by Brahmā and Śaṃkara.
Striding over all the earth, O auspicious daughter of the mountain, / that foot extended a hundred yojanas beyond it.
The eternal one gave divine sight to that king of the Daityas; / Janārdana revealed his own form to him.
Seeing that universal form of the god, Bali, the lord of the Daityas, / attained incomparable joy, flooded with tears of bliss.
Seeing the god, bowing down, and praising him with hymns of praise, / he spoke in a choked voice, with a joyful inner self.

Bali said:
"I am blessed, I have achieved my purpose, having seen you, the Supreme Lord! / Take this triple world yourself, O Supreme Lord!"

Śrī Śaṃkara said:
Then Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, the imperishable Acyuta, / extended his second foot upward as far as the world of Brahmā.
Endowed with stars and planets, and surrounded by all the gods, / it was completely filled by the foot of Acyuta, O fair-faced one.
Then Brahmā, the grandfather, with a heart overflowing with joy, / [seeing] that foot of the God of gods marked with the disc, lotus, and other signs,
Saying, "I am blessed!" Brahmā took his own water-pot, / and with devotion washed [the foot] with the water contained therein.
That water became inexhaustible through the power of that Viṣṇu; / that sacred bathing place, that pure water, fell upon the peak of Meru.
For the purification of the world, it flowed in four directions, / as the Sitā, the Alakanandā, the Cakṣu, and the Bhadrā, in due order.
And from there the Alakanandā is known [to flow] south of Meru, / threefold in name, flowing through three paths, having three streams, purifier of the world.
In heaven it is called the Mandākinī, and below, the Bhogavatī; / in the middle [is] the swift-flowing Gaṅgā, auspicious for the purification of men.
Seeing her flowing through the middle of Meru, O fair-faced one, / I bore her upon my head for my own purification.
Having borne the auspicious water of the Gaṅgā for a thousand divine years, / I attained auspiciousness (śivatva), O goddess, worshiped in all the worlds.
Whoever carries on his head the water of the Gaṅgā born from the foot of Viṣṇu, / or sips it, will become revered by the world; there is no doubt.
Whoever says "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā," even from hundreds of yojanas away, / is freed from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Then King Bhagīratha and Gautama of great ascetic power, / having worshiped me with austerities, begged me for the Gaṅgā.
For the welfare of all worlds, that auspicious Vaiṣṇava Gaṅgā, / that best of rivers, I gave to both of them with love, O goddess.
Brought by Gautama, it was celebrated as the Gautamī; / it became known as the Bhāgīrathī because it was chosen by that king.
In connection with this, the unsurpassed birth of the Gaṅgā has been recounted to you. / Then the glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is affectionate to his devotees,
Gave to Bali, the lord of the Daityas, the auspicious world of Rasātala, / and over all the Dānavas, Nāgas, and aquatic creatures,
He made Bali the king until the dissolution of the universe. / Having accepted the worlds from Bali in the guise of a young student, the slayer of Daityas,
The son of Kaśyapa, the imperishable Viṣṇu, gladly gave them to Mahendra. / Then the gods together with the Gandharvas and the sages of great splendor
Praised Acyuta with divine hymns of praise and worshiped him. / Having contracted that immense form so that they could behold him,
Hari, being worshiped by the thirty gods, vanished. / In this way Śakra was well protected by Viṣṇu, the mighty ruler;

The lord of the three heavens regained the great sovereignty of the three worlds. / All this auspicious glory of Vāmana has been recounted to you; / the rest of the glory, O goddess, I shall relate in due order."

6.241.m:
The Lord said:
There was a great son of Bhṛgu, Jamadagni, the best of the twice-born, / who had mastered all the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, and was of great ascetic power.
That righteous one performed austerities directed toward Mahendra, O passionate lady, / for the duration of a thousand years on the auspicious bank of the Gaṅgā.

Then, being pleased, the Lord, the chastiser of Pāka, Indra, spoke.
Indra said:
"Choose a boon, O chief of brahmins, whatever is in your heart."

The Lord said:
Then the brahmin sage spoke to Śatakratu, who was fully pleased.
Jamadagni said:
"O god, give me Surabhi, who always yields all desires."

The Lord said:
Then the lord of the gods, the splitter of mountains, being pleased with that brahmin, / gave the goddess Surabhi, who yields all desires, at that time.
Having obtained the goddess Surabhi, Jamadagni of great ascetic power / lived possessing great lordliness, like a second Śatakratu.
Jamadagni of great ascetic power married according to the prescribed rite / the charming daughter of Reṇuka, named Reṇukā.
Along with her, that righteous one delighted for many years, / just as the powerful Saṃkrandana with the auspicious goddess Paulomī.
Then, desiring a son, that very righteous one performed a sacrifice; / through the sacrifice he satisfied the Lord, the chastiser of Pāka.
The husband of Śacī, fully pleased, [granted] to him a son of great strength, / of great splendor, mighty-armed, the scorcher of all enemies.
Then in time, the chief of brahmins begot upon Reṇukā, O lady of bright smiles, / a son of great prowess, endowed with strength,
Characterized by all auspicious marks, by a portion of a portion of Viṣṇu. / When that son of great prowess was born, Bhṛgu, his grandfather,
Gave him a name with joy, marked as a portion of Viṣṇu; / he made his auspicious name "Rāma."
Born from Jamadagni, he was called Jāmadagnya; / that bull among the twice-born, belonging to the lineage of Bhṛgu, grew up.
Initiated by him and versed in all branches of learning, / he then went to the Śālagrāma mountain to perform austerities.
There he saw Kaśyapa, the brāhmaṇa seer of boundless radiance; / filled with joy toward him, that twice-born son of Marīci
duly gave him the imperishable Vaiṣṇava mantra. / Having received the mantra then from the great-souled Kaśyapa, Rāma
duly worshipped the husband of Kamalā at that time, / continually chanting the great six-syllable mantra day and night,
meditating on Viṣṇu, Hari, the lotus-petal-eyed and all-pervading. / For many years that righteous descendant of Bhṛgu performed austerities.
With his senses conquered and his speech restrained, the great ascetic stood there. / Meanwhile, the priestly seer Jamadagni remained on the auspicious bank of the Gaṅgā.
He duly performed great righteous deeds, such as sacrifices and gifts; / by the grace of Indra's cow, his riches were complete.
Now after some time, the lordly sovereign of the Haihayas, / having conquered all realms, surrounded by all his armies,
reached the hermitage of the Bhārgava Jamadagni. / Seeing that fortunate one, the king bowed to the best of sages.
Having inquired about the well-being of that great seer of purified spirit, / the king gave him garments and ornaments.
And he duly honoured the king who had come to his house: / having honoured the best of kings with the honey-mixture,
the sage provided a meal for the lord of kings along with his army. / Surabhi was petitioned by that wise descendant of Bhṛgu;
Śabalā then produced an abundance of food, drink, and other provisions. / The inexhaustible food, drink, and other things brought forth by her, the great ascetic,
the best of sages, presented to the lord of kings and his army. / Seeing that Śabalā, the king was filled with curiosity;
very evil-minded, he conceived a desire for that cow. / The best of kings begged Jamadagni for Surabhi there.
Kārttavīrya said: / 'O brāhmaṇa, give me Śabalā, the tawny cow who grants all desires! / I shall give you thousands of other cows, O you of noble vows!'
Īśvara said: / Thus addressed by that king, Jamadagni of great austerities replied. / Jamadagni said: / 'Śabalā is not to be given by me to you, O king, O lord of the earth!
Moreover, she is protected by the god of gods, Śakra. / How could the wealth of the gods be given away by me, O king?'
Īśvara said: / Thus addressed, that king, defiled by anger, / seized Śabalā by force, surrounded by his entire army.
Thereupon the highly fortunate Śabalā, of fair complexion, grew enraged; / she struck down his troops with her horns and the soles of her hooves.
Having slain that army by force in a moment, / the divine cow vanished and instantly went into the presence of Śakra.
Seeing his army slain, Arjuna became swooning with rage; / with his fist he struck the Bhārgava, the best of the twice-born.
Struck repeatedly by him, his limbs were crippled; / suddenly the best of the twice-born fell to the earth and died.
Having killed the best of sages there, the evil-natured ruler of the Haihayas, / escorted by his great host, entered his own city.
Meanwhile Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, worshipped the lord of the gods of gods; / worshipped by him, the god Keśava, pleased, spoke:
The Blessed Lord said: / 'I am pleased with your austerity, my child, since your self is restrained. / I shall bestow upon you, O brāhmaṇa, my supreme, auspicious power.
Then, entered by my power, slay the wicked leaders of kings, / to destroy the earth’s burden and indeed for the welfare of the gods.'

Īśvara said: / Having spoken thus, the god gave him an axe that overpowers enemies, / the great Vaiṣṇava bow, and numerous celestial weapons. / Having given them, the blessed Janārdana said to the son of Jamadagni:
The Blessed Lord said: / 'Slaying the kings arrogant with pride many times over, slayer of enemy heroes, / take possession of the whole earth bounded by the oceans, O best of the twice-born!
And rule it according to dharma, endowed with great valour. / In time, through my grace, you shall also attain my abode.'
Īśvara said: / Having spoken thus and granted the boon to the twice-born, the god vanished. / Then Rāma quickly departed for his father's hermitage.
Seeing his father slain, the Bhārgava swooned with rage; / desiring to rid the earth filled with kings of the kṣatriya class,
he went to the city of the lord of the Haihayas, which was crowded with kings; / with limbs blazing in a seizure of wrath, he stood at the gate with uplifted weapons.
Seeing him, the son of Jamadagni of mighty radiance, the people of that city / thought him to be like the fire of cosmic dissolution, blazing with his bodily form.
Afflicted with terror, they all fled and reported to the king, the lord of the Haihayas, / about that being of great courage, equipped with all weapons.
Having heard their words, that king said with an astonished mind: / The lord of the Haihayas said: / 'Who is this that stands by force, armed, at the gate of my city?
Be it Mahendra, Yama, Rudra, or Dhanada, / none is able to stand armed at the gate of my city at any time!'
Mahādeva said: / Having spoken thus, that lord of kings dispatched very powerful servants / to see him; 'Seize him!' said the evil-minded one.
They went and saw the mighty hero at the city gate, / hard to gaze upon by reason of his splendour, like the blazing fire of cosmic dissolution.
Those very strong ones were unable even to gaze upon him there; / yet, wishing to seize that hero, they rushed forth aggressively from all sides.
Seeing all those armed servants of the lord of kings, / the best of brāhmaṇas, the son of Jamadagni of mighty strength, smiled and spoke.
Paraśurāma said: / 'I, Rāma, son of the Bhārgava, have arrived, O lowest of men! / Because of my father's death, I shall slay all the foremost of kings.
I shall offer Kārtavīrya's blood, mixed with sesame, to my father, / and the funeral ball with the lotus of his head!'
Mahādeva said: / Thus addressed, those servants of that king, possessing great heroism, / struck him with arrows as one might strike fire with straw.
Thereupon the exceedingly heroic Rāma of true valour, enraged, / drew the Vaiṣṇava bow and made the bowstring resound.
By that mighty sound the three worlds were filled; / even for the gods there arose a great, wondrous terror.
Then with swift arrows resembling fire, the exceedingly mighty one / struck those heroic, very strong servants.
Having slain the servants of that great king, / he stood like the fire of cosmic dissolution, terrifying to all beings.
Hearing that his servants had been slain by the wise Rāma, / the heroic lord of the Haihayas, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
went forth with his army to where the imperishable Bhārgava stood. / Seeing him of terrible appearance, blazing with his own lustre,
all the people there were terrified, suspecting the destruction of mankind. / Then a most dreadful battle took place between Rāma and the king,
with terrible discharges of weapons and missiles, like two raining clouds. / Then Rāma of great splendour / effortlessly consumed that king's entire army in a moment with the Vaiṣṇava weapon.
Then, with his sharp battle-axe, Rāma of boundless valour / [attacked the king] ...
he cut off the thousand arms of the evil-minded Kārttavīrya. / The great, heroic king was unable to fight with Rāma.
His strength gone on account of his own sin, the evil-minded one was defeated there; / the wrathful, mighty son of Reṇukā cut off his head,
just as the mighty lord of the gods cuts off a great mountain-peak with his thunderbolt. / Having slain that thousand-armed one, the glorious son of Jamadagni
slew all kings in battle, enraged, with his axe. / Seeing Rāma exceedingly fierce, the kings on the face of the earth
all fled, afflicted with fear, like elephants fleeing a lion. / Even as the rulers of the earth fled, through fury over his father's death
the enraged Bhārgava killed them, as the king of birds kills serpents. / The glorious son of Jamadagni rid the entire earth of Kṣatriyas.
The blessed one spared only the great lineage of Ikṣvāku, / because it was his maternal grandfather's lineage, and at the word of Reṇukā.
Depriving of their kingdoms those born of the maternal grandfather's lineage, / Rāma, the ender of royal dynasties, did not slay those descendants of Manu.
Indeed, the valiant one destroyed the entire lineage of all other kings. / Making the earth entirely devoid of Kṣatriyas, the mighty son of Jamadagni,
a twice-born, duly performed the great horse sacrifice, / and granted the earth with its seven continents to the foremost of the Brahmins.
Having granted the earth to the Brahmins, the glorious son of Jamadagni / then went to the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa to practice austerities.
This has been told to you, O goddess: the deed of the noble son of Jamadagni, / the power-empowered incarnation of the bow-wielding Lord.

Indeed, he is not to be worshipped [as supreme] because of being a power-empowered [manifestation] of the Great Soul; / [rather,] the two who are to be worshipped by the devotees of the Lord and by noble, foremost Brahmins
are the incarnations Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, complete with excellent qualities, / worshipped by the sages, bestowers of liberation unto mortals.

6.242.m: Rudra said: / Formerly, Manu Svāyambhuva chanted the great twelve-syllable mantra / on the bank of the Gomatī, in pure and auspicious Naimiṣa.
By him the Lord of Kamalā was worshipped for a thousand years. / The blessed Lord Hari said to him: 'Choose a boon from Me.'
Then Manu Svāyambhuva joyfully said to Hari: / Manu said: 'O Lord of gods, O Acyuta, take up sonship [to me] across three births;
with a longing for a son I worship You, the Supreme Person.' / Rudra said: / Spoken to thus by him, the Lord of Lakṣmī replied with a great voice.
Viṣṇu said: / 'O best of kings, what is desired in your heart will come to pass. / I Myself have a great affection to be your son.
At the times required for the preservation [of the universe], here and there, O best of kings, / when you are born, I too am born as your [son], O you of noble vows.
For the protection of the good and for the destruction of evildoers, / for the establishment of dharma, I come into being, O sinless one.'
Rudra said: / Having granted him the boon in this way, Hari disappeared right there. / And of that Manu Svāyambhuva, the first birth came to be:
formerly in the lineage of the Raghus he was King Daśaratha; / his second [birth] was as the mighty Vasudeva in the lineage of the Vṛṣṇis.
In the final quarters of Kali, which measures a thousand divine years, / reaching the village of Śambhala, he will be born as a Brahmin.
Kauśalyā became the wife of King Daśaratha; / for the service of Yadu's lineage, she was renowned by the name Devakī;
and next she will be Devaprabhā, the wife of the Brahmin Harivrata. / Thus she attains motherhood across three births of the Wielder of the Bow.
First I shall relate to you the deeds of Rāma, O lady of noble vows, / by the mere remembrance of which even sinners attain liberation.
Entering upon their second birth, Hiraṇyaka and Hiraṇyākṣa / were born as the exceedingly powerful Kumbhakarṇa and the Ten-necked One.
The son of Pulastya was the righteous Brahmin named Viśravas; / his wife, O sinless one, was large-eyed, the daughter of a king of the rākṣasas.
She was the daughter of Sukeśa and the demon Sumālī; / that maiden was named Kekasī, his wife of firm vows.
Overcome with desire, that goddess, slender-limbed and fair to behold, / made love at twilight with the great sage to her heart's content.
Because of passion and because of conceiving at twilight, two sons of great strength were born of her: / Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa, rākṣasas renowned throughout the world.
A daughter named Śūrpaṇakhā was born, hideous of face. / Then, after some time, Vibhīṣaṇa was born of her:
of good character, devoted to the Lord, truthful of speech, righteous, and pure. / Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa, on the excellent mountain Himavat,
worshipped Me intensely with extremely severe austerities. / But then the evil-souled Rāvaṇa, with the beautiful lotuses of his own heads,
worshipped Me, O goddess, by that very frightful act. / Then, O fair-browed one, with a delighted heart I said to him:
'Choose a boon from Me, my child, whatever is in your mind.' / Then the evil-souled one said, wishing to conquer all worlds:
'Grant me invulnerability against gods, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas.' / Then I granted to that evil-souled rākṣasa
invulnerability against gods, Dānavas, and Yakṣas, O fair-faced one. / Arrogant from the granting of that boon, that rākṣasa of great valour
tormented the three worlds—gods, Dānavas, and humans. / Oppressed by him, the gods led by Brahmā,
afflicted by fear, went for refuge to the Lord, the husband of Kamalā. / Then, understanding their suffering, the Eternal One, to grant them fearlessness,
spoke to all the thirty gods, headed by Brahmā and Rudra: / The Blessed Lord said: 'I will be born in the lineage of Raghu, to King Daśaratha;
I will slay the evil-minded Rāvaṇa along with his kinsmen. / Assuming a human form, I shall slay that thorn of the gods.
And you, by Nandi's curse having become monkeys, / help Me, O best of Gandharvas and Apsarases!'
Rudra said: / Spoken to thus by Viṣṇu, the God of gods, all the deities / took the form of monkeys and were born on the surface of the earth.
The earth, ocean-girdled, given away by the Bhārgava, / was formerly given by the great sages to the noble Raghus.
The son of Manu Vaivasvata, best among kings, of great power, / was renowned as Ikṣvāku, foremost among knowers of all dharma.
In his lineage was the glorious, mighty King Daśaratha, / the son of King Aja, truthful, virtuous, and pure.
That king ruled the whole earth through his valour; / he established all the excellent kings in their kingdoms.
Then that king wedded a maiden, beautiful in every limb, / the daughter of the king of Kośala, named Kauśalyā.
And the daughter of the king of Magadha, sweetly smiling, / Sumitrā by name, was his second lovely wife.
The daughter of the king of Kekaya then became the third / wife, lotus-petal-eyed, named Kaikeyī.
With those three wives, that righteous descendant of Kakutstha / delighted himself while protecting the earth.

There was a city named Ayodhyā situated on the bank of the Sarayū,
filled with all kinds of jewels, teeming with wealth and grain,

attended by ramparts and gateways, crowded with golden walls,
with excellent elephants and horses, like the city of Mahendra.

In it, that righteous king dwelt with the best of sages,
with his family priest, the twice-born, noble-souled Vasiṣṭha.

He ruled his entire kingdom, having eliminated all thorns,
because the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Person, was to be born in it.

Therefore that sacred city is celebrated as Ayodhyā;
its name was also that of the supreme abode of the city, O fair one.

Where the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu abides, that alone is the supreme abode;
there immediate liberation takes place, severing all karmas.

When Mahāviṣṇu was born there, all men were filled with joy.
That king, having ruled the whole earth, O fair-faced one,

desiring a son, sacrificed with a Vaiṣṇava offering to Hari, the Infallible.
Worshipped by him, the Lord of Śrī, Hari, who is all-pervading,

granting boons through that Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, Keśava spoke.
Then Hari, in the form of sacrifice, appeared in that fire,

resembling pure gold, holding a conch, discus, and mace,
wearing white garments, glorious, adorned with all ornaments,

his chest bearing the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha, adorned with a garland of forest flowers,
large-eyed like lotus petals, four-armed, of noble intellect.

Together with Śrī seated on his left hip, the Lord of Ramā appeared.
Affectionate toward his devotees, he said to the king: “I am the giver of boons.”

Seeing that Lord of all the worlds, the king was overwhelmed with joy;
together with his wife, with an inner self overjoyed, he bowed down.

Having bowed with folded hands, with a voice faltering with joy,
he said to the God of gods, Janārdana: “Become my son.”

Then the gracious Lord, the Infallible, said to the king:
Viṣṇu said: “O best of kings, I shall indeed be born for the welfare of the world of gods,

for the protection of the virtuous, and for the destruction of the rākṣasas,
to grant liberation to the worlds, and to establish dharma.”

Mahādeva said:
Having said this, Hari gave to the king divine cooked milk-rice,
placed in a golden vessel, pure, in the hand of Lakṣmī.

Mahādeva said:
Having spoken thus, praised by all the sages,
Janārdana, having revealed his own form, then vanished in that very way.

Seeing his eldest and youngest wives there,
that king, fully composed, divided the divine milk-rice and gave it to them.

At that moment, his middle wife Sumitrā,
fair-eyed and desiring a son, approached him.

Seeing her there, Kauśalyā and the slender-waisted Kaikeyī
both gave half of their own milk-rice to her.

Having eaten that divine milk-rice, the king's slender-waisted wives,
having all become pregnant, shone with bright splendor.

In their dreams, the Lord of gods, Janārdana, dressed in yellow garments,
Hari, with conch, discus, and mace in hand, then appeared.

At this delightful time, in the month of Madhu, O purely smiling one,
on the bright ninth lunar day, in the spotless asterism dedicated to Aditi,

at noon, at the ascendant endowed with auspiciousness from all planets,
Kauśalyā gave birth to a son, Hari, the Lord of the world:

dark like the petal of a blue lotus, resembling ten million gods of love,
large-eyed like lotus petals, adorned with all ornaments,

his chest bearing the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha, adorned with all ornaments,
shining with ear-rings resembling the rising sun,

resembling many suns, surrounded by great splendor,
the delightful body of the Supreme Lord, like a lamp produced from a lamp,

the Lord of all worlds, to be meditated upon by yogins, eternal,
the meaning of all the Upaniṣads, the infinite, supreme ruler,

the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, disease-free,
the refuge of all beings, omnipresent, composed of all beings.

When the Lord of the universe was born, divine kettledrums sounded in the sky,
and the best of gods showered showers of flowers.

The gods headed by Prajāpati, situated in aerial chariots in the vault of the sky,
along with the sages, praised him, overwhelmed with limbs full of joy.

The Gandharva lords sang, and the celestial nymphs danced;
sacred and auspicious winds blew; the sun shone brightly;

the fires burned pacified, and the ten directions were spotless.
Then that king, having seen the eternal son with joy,

then performed the birth-rites with the family priest Vasiṣṭha.
And the venerable Vasiṣṭha then gave him a delightful name:

“This great lord is the delight of Śrī, who dwells in the lotus;
therefore his ancient name is established as Śrīrāma.

It is equal to the thousand names of the Lord of Śrī, granting liberation to men.
Because he is born equal to Viṣṇu, he is called Viṣṇu.”

Thus having given him this name, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha,
circumambulating, bowing down, and praising him with hymns,

reciting the thousand names for the auspiciousness of the noble-souled one,
went forth in great splendor from that most sacred house.

Then the king gladly gave much wealth to the foremost twice-born,
and in accordance with dharma gave gifts of ten thousand cows.

The best of Raghu's line gave a hundred thousand villages,
with garments, divine ornaments, and innumerable riches.

To please Viṣṇu, he gratified the Brahmins there.
And Kauśalyā, having seen her son Rāma, lotus-eyed,

shining like a blossoming hand-lotus, endowed with lotus hands and feet,
on his glorious lotus-feet—the lotus and water-lily, O fair-faced one—

marked with conch, discus, mace, lotus, banner, and cloth,
and seeing on his chest the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha with the forest garland,

the large-eyed one [saw] in his body the entire universe with gods, asuras, and men,
and the fourteen worlds in his smiling mouth;

she saw the Vedas along with legendary histories in the breath of that noble-souled one,
and continents, oceans, and mountains on his hips, O fair-complexioned one;

in his navel Brahmā and Śiva, and in his ears the auspicious directions;
in his eyes fire and the sun, and in his nose the wind of great speed.

Seeing all his glorious manifestations, the meaning of all the Upaniṣads,
the beautiful-hipped woman, terrified, bowed again and again,
and with eyes filled with tears of joy, with folded hands, she spoke these words:

Kauśalyā said:
“Blessed am I, O God of gods, O Lord, having obtained you as a son.
Be gracious to me, O Lord of the universe; display filial affection!”

Īśvara said:
Addressed in this way by his mother, Hṛṣīkeśa, the all-pervading Hari,
assuming an illusory human form, wept out of babyhood.

Then the delighted lady Kauśalyā, endowed with auspicious marks,
embracing her son with joy, the slender-waisted one gave her breast.

The eternal God drank her breast milk out of babyhood;
the maintainer of the universe, the great all-pervading Lord, dwelt on his mother's lap.

In that delightful country, brilliant and granting all desires to men,
the citizens and the people of the countryside made festival with joy.
In Kaikeyī was born Bharata, impelled by a portion of Pāñcajanya. / Sumitrā gave birth to Lakṣmaṇa, who possessed auspicious marks,
and to Śatrughna, that illustrious lady [giving birth to] the tormentor of the enemies of the gods. / Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, was born from a portion of Ananta,
and Śatrughna, of boundless prowess, was born from a portion of Sudarśana. / They all grew up there in the lineage of Vaivasvata Manu.
Those sons were duly consecrated by Vasiṣṭha of great splendor. / They all studied the Vedas and became learned, as did the princes,
knowing the true meaning of all scriptures and accomplished in the science of archery. / They became exceedingly generous, increasing the joy of the worlds.
There the two kings, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, became a pair; / likewise, Bharata and Śatrughna formed a pair.
Then Lakṣmī, the sovereign of the worlds, in the dwelling of Janaka, / in an auspicious field, turned up by the plow, in an auspicious furrow at an auspicious moment,
resembling ten million morning suns, with lotus-hands like red water lilies, / endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with all ornaments,
the lovely-limbed one wearing on her breast an unfading lotus garland, / appeared at the furrow's opening in the form of a beautiful child.
Seeing that auspicious maiden embodying the Vedas, / King Janaka, the lord of Mithilā, raised her and nurtured her as his own child.
In the delightful house of Janaka, the beloved of the Lord of all worlds, / the goddess of the gods, grew for the protection of the whole universe.
Meanwhile, O goddess, the world-renowned Kauśika, / in the greatly holy Siddhāśrama on the auspicious bank of the Bhāgīrathī,
the great sage undertook to perform an excellent sacrifice. / Then, as that sacrifice of the twice-born was underway,
the night-roaming demons of Rāvaṇa became destroyers of the sacrifice. / Then Kauśika, contemplating Hari born in Raghu's line,
the righteous-minded one desired to bring him for the welfare of the worlds. / Having gone to the delightful city of Ayodhyā, protected by the descendant of Raghu,
the best of sages saw the foremost king, Daśaratha. / Seeing Kauśika, the king also stood up with folded hands,
and along with his sons, the highly lustrous one bowed to the best of sages. / Saying, "I am blessed," with joy to the descendant of Raghu,
he honored him according to rule after seating him on an excellent seat. / Having led him round and bowed to him, he said to him, "What may I do?"
Then Viśvāmitra of great austerities, his soul delighted, spoke: / Viśvāmitra said: "Give me the descendant of Raghu, O king, for the protection of my sacrifice.
Let there be success for my sacrifice by the presence of the descendant of Raghu; / therefore, you ought to grant Rāma for protection, O ornament [of kings]."
The Lord said: / Hearing that speech of the best of sages, the king, foremost among the omniscient, / gave Rāghava along with Lakṣmaṇa to the best of sages.
Taking Rāghava there, Viśvāmitra of great austerities, / the best of the twice-born, set out for his own hermitage, delighted.
Then the thirty gods, overjoyed when the best of the Raghus set forth, / rained showers of flowers and praised [them], being of great luster.
Then Garuḍa of great strength arrived with a delighted mind; / invisible to beings, having approached the best of the Raghus,
having given them two celestial bows, two quivers with inexhaustible arrows, / and celestial weapons and missiles, the bird departed.
To those two heroes, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, as they were going in the forest, / a hideous-looking rākṣasa woman was pointed out by the high-souled Kauśika,
by name Tāḍakā, O goddess, the wife of the rākṣasa Sunda. / The two great heroes slew her with arrows shot from their celestial bows.
Slain then by Rāghava, that hideous-looking rākṣasa woman, / abandoning her dreadful body, assumed a celestial form.
Blazing with her body and adorned with all ornaments, / she bowed to the two best of Raghus and went to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having slain her, the glorious Rāghava, of great splendor, / entered the auspicious hermitage of Kauśika along with the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa.
Then the joyful sages went out to meet the best of the Raghus, / seated him, and worshipped the Supreme Self with water for hospitality and the like.
Kauśika, having undertaken the initiation to perform the unexcelled sacrifice, / the best of sages commenced it together with the sages according to rule.
While the great sacrifice was underway, the rākṣasa named Mārīca, / together with his brother Subāhu, stood there to cause disruption.
Seeing those two dreadful rākṣasas, Rāghava, the slayer of enemy heroes, / struck down Subāhu, the lord of rākṣasas, with a single arrow.
With the great wind-missile, he hurled the night-roamer Mārīca / into the ocean, just as the wind hurls a dry leaf.
Seeing that great prowess of Rāma, that best of rākṣasas, / having laid down his weapons, went to a great hermitage to practice austerities.
When the great sacrifice was completed, Viśvāmitra of great splendor / worshipped Rāghava there with a joyful mind.
Embracing the high-souled Hari, who wore side-locks, / dark like the petal of a blue lotus, with wide eyes like lotus petals,
the best of sages then smelled him on the head and praised him. / In the meantime, the king, the sovereign of Mithilā,
began to perform the Vājapeya sacrifice with the best of sages. / To see it, they all set out, led by Viśvāmitra,
the sages of pure heart accompanied by the tiger among the Raghus. / As that high-souled Rāma was going, by his lotus-foot
that ground where a great stone was trodden upon became purifying. / She who had been cursed formerly by her husband, the twice-born Gautama,
Ahalyā, became auspicious from the touch of the foot of the lord of the Raghus. / Then, having reached the city of Mithilā, the best of sages,
accompanied by the two descendants of Raghu, became delighted in their minds. / Seeing those illustrious ones who had arrived, the king of great strength,
going out to meet them and bowing, the lord of Mithilā then honored / Rāma, who had large lotus-like eyes and the luster of a blue lotus petal,
wearing yellow garments, delicate, radiant with tender limbs, / who surpassed the beauty of ten million gods of love, the highest one,
endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with all ornaments, / who is Hari, the body of the supreme Lord within the center of one's lotus heart,
arisen like a lamp from a lamp, endowed with supreme virtues such as good conduct. / Seeing that lord of the Raghus, Janaka, joyful at heart,
regarded that Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, as none other than the supreme Lord. / Saying, "I am blessed," the king worshipped the descendant of Kakutstha.
The ruler of men regarded it as the grace of Vāsudeva Viṣṇu, / and the lord resolved in his mind to give his daughter to him.
Knowing them to be the two sons of Raghu's race, the best of kings there / honored them according to dharma with garments and auspicious ornaments.
He worshipped the ṛṣis with honors such as the honey-mixture offering. / Then, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the lotus-eyed Rāma,
having broken the celestial bow of Śiva, won the daughter of Janaka. / Then he, satisfied by that great bride-price of valor,
the lord of Mithilā joyfully gave the earth-born maiden to him, / just as formerly the great ocean gave Śrī to Keśava.
The lord of Mithilā dispatched a messenger to the descendant of Raghu; / and the righteous-souled [king] entered Mithilā with his two sons.
Along with Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and other delighted sages, that king, / the foremost of the Raghus, dwelt in Janaka's delightful city.
At that very auspicious time, the king, honored by the king of Mithilā, / performed Rāma's marriage with the daughter of the earth.
He gave to Lakṣmaṇa the maiden named Urmilā, born of Janaka; / and then, the two daughters of Janaka's younger brother, of auspicious radiance,
Māṇḍavī and Śrutakīrti, endowed with all auspicious marks— / the king arranged their marriages to Bharata and Saumitri.
Having concluded the wedding rites there, the mighty and glorious King Daśaratha / set out for Ayodhyā, accompanied by citizens and countrymen,
having accepted the wedding gifts and having been honored by the king of Mithilā, / accompanied by his sons, his daughters-in-law, horses, elephants, and retinue of forces.
On that path, the mighty and glorious Jāmadagnya, / grasping his axe and bow, like an enraged lion,
charged toward Kākutstha, wishing to fight, that destroyer of kings. / Having reached and seen Rāghava, Bhārgava addressed these words:
Paraśurāma said: / 'O Rāma, Rāma, mighty-armed one, hear my word: / having slain kings of great valor many times in battle,
and having given the earth to the brahmins, I went to practice austerities. / Having heard of your valor and power, I have come here to fight with you.
Descendants of Ikṣvāku are not to be slain by me, since they are born of my maternal grandfather's lineage. / Yet, having heard of your valor and kṣatriya power, I cannot bear it,
since the dread and unassailable bow was broken by you, O king! / Therefore, O best of the Raghus, give me a generous battle!
Or rather, string this Vaiṣṇava bow, equal to that [former] one, O subduer of foes, / by your valor; then indeed I shall be conquered by you.
Otherwise, lay down your weapons before me, the mighty one; / take refuge, O Kākutstha, if you are faint-hearted in your mind!'
The Lord said: / Thus addressed by Bhārgava, the glorious Kākutstha / grasped his bow and also his Vaiṣṇava power.
Deprived of his power, the glorious Jāmadagnya then / became powerless, his splendor gone, like a twice-born devoid of rituals.
Seeing Bhārgava deprived of his splendor, the best of kings / praised Kākutstha again and again, saying, 'Excellent, excellent!'
Grasping that great bow and stringing it with ease, / Kākutstha set an arrow upon that bow and said to the astonished Bhārgava:
Rāma said: / 'With this foremost arrow, what should be done for you, O twice-born? / Shall I sever this lower world, or heaven, or destroy your austerities?'
The Lord said: / Seeing that terrifying arrow of Rāma, / and realizing that he was the Supreme Self, Bhārgava, overjoyed, said to Rāma:
Paraśurāma said: / 'O Rāma, Rāma, mighty-armed one, I did not know you as the eternal one. / Today indeed I know, O Kākutstha, through your valor, virtues, and the like.
You are the primal Person incarnate, the supreme Brahman, the transcendent, imperishable one. / You are Ananta, Mahāviṣṇu, Vāsudeva, higher than the highest.
You are Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Lord, the embodiment of the three Vedas. / You are Time, you are the entire universe, and you are named the syllable "A".
Creator, sustainer, and destroyer, you alone are the supreme Lord. / You are inconceivable, having the form of the Great Being; you are the great Manu.
Possessing four, six, and five qualities, you alone are the Supreme Person. / You are the sacrifice, you are the vaṣaṭ utterance, you are the syllable Oṃ, consisting of the three Vedas.
Manifest and unmanifest in nature, bearer of the qualities, yet transcendent beyond qualities, / I am unable to praise you, who are beyond the reach even of the Vedas.
The impetuosity that I showed through a desire to fight you, O Lord, / that must be forgiven by you, O master, out of sheer grace.
Having conquered all kings by your power and given the earth to the twice-born, / it is solely by your grace that one attains ultimate peace.'
The Lord said: / Having spoken thus to Kākutstha, Jāmadagnya of great austerities, / circumambulating and bowing down to Rāghava, the protector of the worlds,
offered to that weapon the heavenly realm acquired by performing a hundred sacrifices. / Then Rāghava, possessed of great splendor, paid homage to that great sage
and honored him according to rule with water for the feet, respectful offering, water for sipping, and other rites. / Honored there by him, Jāmadagnya of great austerities
went to the delightful hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa to perform austerities. / Then that mighty King Daśaratha, with his sons accompanied by their wives,
entered his own city at an auspicious moment. / Rāghava, Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Bharata,
approaching their respective wives, rejoiced with delighted minds. / There for twelve years, the righteous Rāghava
delighted with Sītā, as Nārāyaṇa with Śrī. / At that very time, King Daśaratha, the ruler of the earth,
wished out of affection to install his eldest son in the kingship. / Then his beloved wife Kaikeyī, to whom boons had previously been granted,
asked the foremost of kings for Bharata's consecration / and Rāma's exile for fourteen years.
Because of his word of truth, that king then exiled Rāma, / his son, from the kingdom, his senses shattered by grief.
Though capable [of resisting], Rāghava relinquished the kingdom according to dharma / for the sake of slaying the ten-necked one and on account of his father's word.
Kākutstha went to the forest along with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā. / Afflicted by separation from his son and overcome by grief, the king died.
Though urged by the ministers to take that kingdom, / the righteous Bharata did not desire the kingdom, displaying brotherly devotion.
Having come to the forest, he then begged his brother Kākutstha; / but Rāma, the subduer of foes, did not desire the kingdom due to his father's command.
He gave his pair of sandals to him, and he took them with devotion. / Having obtained the two sandals of Rāma for the auspicious kingdom,
the son of Kaikeyī, that foremost of kings, remained there, / worshipping daily with fragrant unguents and flowers, devoted to the practice of austerity.
Until the return of that great-souled Rāghava, / all the inhabitants of the city were devoted to vows.
On Mount Citrakūṭa, in the auspicious hermitage of Bharadvāja, / Rāghava took delight with Vaidehī in the auspicious waters of the Mandākinī.
Once the noble-minded Rāma was sleeping in the lap of Vaidehī; / the crow, son of Indra, arrived and moved about in that very place.
Seeing Jānakī there, afflicted by the arrow of Kāmadeva, / he tore open her plump, elevated breast with his sharp talons.
Seeing that crow, Rāma, the supporter of the earth, took a blade of kuśa grass in his hand, / charged it with the Brahmā weapon, and hurled it.
Seeing that grass blade of terrifying appearance, its form fashioned of flames, / the crow fled, uttering a distressed cry.
Rāma's most dreadful weapon pursued that crow. / The crow roamed through the three worlds, tormented by fear.
Wherever the crow, that bird seeking refuge, went, / right there that weapon entered, inspiring dread.
To Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Yama, and Varuṇa, / the crow, afflicted by the weapon, went swiftly, seeking refuge.
Seeing that crow, all the gods and Dānavas headed by Rudra / said, being wise: “We are not able to save [you].” / Then spoke the blessed Brahmā, lord of the three worlds:

Brahmā said:
“O best of crow-kind, take refuge with him alone. / He alone is the protector, the glorious one, the treasury of compassion for all.
He, the essence of forbearance, fond of his devotees, surely protects those who have come for refuge. / He is the Lord of all beings, endowed with virtues such as good character.
He is the protector of the living world, father, mother, friend, and well-wisher. / Take refuge with the Lord of gods; there is no other refuge, O bird!”

Mahādeva said:
Addressed thus by Brahmā, that crow approached the joy of the Raghus / and suddenly fell to the ground, terrified with fear.
Seeing the crow brought to the risk of its life, Sītā then / said to her husband, the Lord, out of compassion: “Save it, save it!”
To the crow that had fallen on the earth in front of them, / the daughter of Janaka then placed its head at his feet.
Then, having raised it up with his hand, the virtuous Rāma, an ocean of nectar of mercy, / moved with pity, protected the crow.
Rāma, that treasury of compassion, said to that crow: “Do not fear! / I shall grant you freedom from fear; go, go as you please.”
Having bowed repeatedly to Rāghava and to Sītā, / it quickly departed to heaven, protected by Rāghava.
Then Rāma dwelt on Mount Citrakūṭa with Vaidehī / and the wise Lakṣmaṇa, praised by great sages.
Having been honoured there by Bharadvāja, Rāghava, / the best of the Raghus, went to the extensive hermitage of Atri.
Seeing the best of the Raghus arrived, that foremost of eminent sages, / righteous in nature, went forth to meet him along with his wife, filled with joy.
Having seated [him] with Sītā on a foremost, auspicious seat, / [he offered] water for respectful offering, for washing the feet, and for sipping, as well as various garments,
and with love gave the honey-mixture, ornaments, and unguent. / His wife Anasūyā, for her part, [offered] an unexcelled heavenly garment
and gave splendid ornaments to Sītā with love, / and fed Rāghava with divine foods, drinks, sweets, and other provisions.
Honoured there by him with supreme devotion, the king / Rāma dwelt there happily for a day, along with Lakṣmaṇa.
At clear dawn, having risen, circumambulated the great sage, / and bowed down, Rāma set out to depart.
Permitted then by him, the lotus-eyed Rāma / set out for the Daṇḍaka forest, crowded with assemblies of great sages.
Having killed there a dreadful, very terrifying rākṣasa named Virādha, / he then entered the auspicious hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
Having seen the descendant of Kakutstha, his sins immediately destroyed, / he went to the world of Brahmā, accompanied by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
In succession Rāma went to [the hermitages of] Sutīkṣṇa, Agastya, / and Agastya's brother, and was likewise honoured by them.
Then at Pañcavaṭī, on the auspicious bank of the Godāvarī, / Rāma lived for a very long time in supreme happiness.
Having gone there, the best of sages, ascetics practising righteousness, / worshipped the lotus-eyed Rāma, the lord of their self.
And they reported to him their fear caused by the hordes of rākṣasas; / having reassured them, the descendant of Kakutstha granted the gift of safety.
Honoured by him, they went to their respective hermitages; / while he lived there, thirteen years of Rāma's [exile] passed away.
On the delightful bank of the Godāvarī, at lovely Pañcavaṭī, / once upon a time a rākṣasī of terrible form,
the sister of Rāvaṇa, difficult to approach, entered there. / But seeing the foremost of Raghus, resembling ten million gods of love,
dark like the petal of a blue lotus, with eyes broad as lotus petals, / high-shouldered, mighty-armed, with a conch-like neck and a strong jaw,
resembling the full moon, with a smiling lotus-face, / covered with sleek, curly hair resembling swarms of bees,
resembling red lotuses, his lotus-palms bearing auspicious marks, / adorned with a row of nails resembling the unblemished moon,
glowing like sleek, tender dūrvā grass, an auspicious treasury of delicacy, / clad in yellow silk, adorned with all ornaments,
of youthful, tender age, whose form enchants the universe— / seeing that Rāma, the rākṣasī was pierced by the arrows of the god of love.

Approaching Rāma, the lotus-eyed one, she said:
The rākṣasī said:
“Who are you who abide in the Daṇḍaka forest in an ascetic's garb?
And for what purpose have you come to this place, unapproachable because of the rākṣasas? / Tell me quickly the truth; you should not speak a falsehood.”

Maheśvara said:
Addressed thus at that time, Rāma laughed and spoke these words:
Rāma said:
“I am called Rāma, son of King Daśaratha; / this sinless younger brother of mine, armed with a bow, is named Lakṣmaṇa;
and this is my dear wife Sītā, the daughter of Janaka. / By the command of my father's word, I have come here to the forest.
We wander in the great forest out of a wish for the welfare of the ṛṣis. / For what purpose have you come to my hermitage, O beautiful one?

Who are you? In whose family were you born? Tell me all truthfully.”
Maheśvara said:
Addressed thus by Rāma, she, unhesitating, spoke these words:

The rākṣasī said:
“I am the daughter of Viśravas, O king, and the sister of Rāvaṇa, / known by the name of Śūrpaṇakhā in the three worlds.
And this Daṇḍaka forest has been given to me by my brother, O lord. / Devouring assemblies of ṛṣis, I wander in the great forest.
But seeing you, the best of ascetics, pierced by the arrows of the god of love, / I have come, wishing to take pleasure with you, utterly fearless.
You ought to become my husband, O tiger among kings! / I desire to devour this Sītā, your chaste wife, O king.
the glorious Rāma raised his sword and cut off her nose and ears.
Weeping, terrified, her face disfigured, the rākṣasī / quickly entered the abode of Khara and told the conduct of that Rāma.
Accompanied by thousands of rākṣasas, surrounded by Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras, / that slayer of enemies came vehemently to fight Rāghava.
In that dreadful forest, with arrows resembling Death and Kāla, / Rāma effortlessly struck down those massive rākṣasas there.
Khara, Triśiras, and the mighty Dūṣaṇa / he felled in battle with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Having slain all the rākṣasas dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, / honoured by the hosts of gods and praised by great sages,
he dwelt in the Daṇḍaka forest with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa. / Hearing of the slaughter of the rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa was overcome with wrath.
