He came to Janasthāna together with the evil-minded Mārīca. / Having arrived at Pañcavaṭī, that ten-necked rākṣasa,
by means of the deceptive Mārīca in the form of a deer, the demon / lured those two sons of Daśaratha far away from the hermitage,
and carried off Sītā, the wife of Rāma, longing for his own death. / But seeing her being carried off, the mighty Jaṭāyus, king of vultures,
Out of friendship for Rāma, he fought there with that rākṣasa. / Having struck that Rāvaṇa with the strength of his arms, the repeller of foes,
entered the city of Laṅkā, surrounded by many rākṣasas, / having placed the daughter of Janaka in the middle of the Aśoka grove.
Desiring death by Rāma's arrow, he entered his own dwelling. / But Rāma, having slain the rākṣasa Mārīca who had assumed the form of a deer,
then returned there accompanied by his brother, the son of Sumitrā. / Then the son of Daśaratha, learning that his wife had been abducted by the rākṣasa,
tormented by excessive grief, lamented, the great-minded one. / While searching in the forest for Sītā, [he saw] on the path the vulture of great strength,
his feet and wings severed, fallen upon the surface of the earth, / his entire body covered with blood; and having seen him, he was filled with wonder.
The glorious Rāghava asked: 'By whom and why were you desired to be killed?' / The vulture, seeing Rāghava, spoke very feebly:

The vulture said:
'O Rāma, your wife was abducted by the mighty Rāvaṇa; / by that foremost of rākṣasas I was struck down in battle.'

Maheśvara said:
Having spoken thus before Rāghava, he suddenly departed this life. / Rāma performed his funeral rites according to the Vedic injunctions,
and granted him his own eternal realm, accessible to yogins. / By the grace of Rāghava, that vulture [attained] the supreme realm;
the best of birds attained liberation, having the same form as Hari. / Then going to Mālyavat, to the auspicious hermitage of Mataṅga,
approaching the highly fortunate Śabarī, who practised dharma— / that foremost of devotees of Bhagavān, seeing Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
came forward to meet them, bowed down, seated them on a seat of kuśa grass, / washed their feet, and with fragrant wild flowers,
she worshipped them with devotion, her mind filled with joy. / Fragrant fruits and sweet roots
the woman of firm vows then offered to the two Rākṣasas. / Tasting the fruits, the descendant of Kakutstha granted her supreme liberation.
Then, having gone to Lake Pampā, Rāghava, the slayer of his foes, / struck down there the rākṣasa Kabandha, of terrifying form.
Having slain him, the one of great valor burned him, and he went to heaven. / Then going to the Godāvarī, the lotus-eyed Rāma
asked: 'O Gaṅgā, do you know of Sītā, my beloved?' / Then, enveloped in darkness, that Gaṅgā did not tell him.
Rāghava in anger cursed her: 'Become water of blood!' / Then, agitated with fear, placing the great sages before her,
with folded hands, she, wretched, sought refuge with Rāghava. / Then all the great sages spoke to the eternal Rāma.

The sages said:
'The Gaṅgā is born from your lotus-feet, the purifier of the three worlds. / You alone, O Lord of the Universe, ought to release her from the curse.'

6.242.m:
Maheśvara said:
Then the righteous Rāma, affectionate to those seeking refuge, spoke:
Rāma said:
'By the mere bathing of Śabarī, united with auspicious water, / let this sin-destroying Gaṅgā be freed from my curse.'
Having spoken thus, the descendant of Kakutstha of great might made that excellent Śabarītīrtha / equal to the Gaṅgā and Gayā with the tip of his bow Śārṅga.
And for the great devotees of the Lord, a sacred bathing place was formed in whose water, / that body will become worshipful to the world, there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, the descendant of Kakutstha went to Mount Ṛṣyamūka. / Then, on the shore of Lake Pampā, by the monkey Hanūmat
he was met, and at his word he came together with Sugrīva. / At the word of Sugrīva, having slain Vālin, the lord of monkeys,
Rāma consecrated Sugrīva in that very kingdom. / And he, wishing to see the daughter of Janaka, dispatched
the heroic monkeys headed by Hanūmat, the lord of monkeys. / Having crossed the ocean, Hanūmān, the son of the Wind,
entered the city of Laṅkā and saw Sītā of firm vows, / emaciated by fasting, miserable, deeply absorbed in grief,
her limbs smeared with dirt and mud, wearing soiled garments. / Presenting the sign of recognition, he reported the news,
[and] there the monkey himself, uprooting a pillar of the gateway, / struck down seven sons of ministers as well as the son of Rāvaṇa.
Having consoled the princess of Videha, he then destroyed the grove, / and the forest-guards, the servants, and the five army commanders.
Then, captured voluntarily by the son of Rāvaṇa, / and having seen the lord of rākṣasas and likewise conversed with him,
the monkey burned the city of Laṅkā with the fire of his own tail; / taking the token of recognition given by her, he came back.
Approaching Rāma of lotus eyes, the mighty leader of monkeys / reported truly: 'Sītā has been seen.'

Accompanied by Sugrīva and surrounded by many monkeys, Rāma / went to the shore of the great ocean and encamped the army there.

The younger brother of Rāvaṇa was known as Vibhīṣaṇa, / righteous, true to his word, and the foremost of the great devotees of the Lord.
knowing that Rāma had arrived, abandoned his elder brother, / his kingdom, sons, and wives, and went for refuge to Rāghava.
And the Lord Rāma, accepting him at the word of the son of the Wind, / having given him reassurance from fear, the gentle one consecrated him in the kingdom of the rakṣases.
Then the descendant of Kakutstha, wishing to cross the ocean, took refuge; / but seeing it with perfectly clear water, the mighty Rāma,
taking up Śārṅga, dried up the ocean with streams of arrows. / Then the lord of rivers, approaching the descendant of Kakutstha, the ocean of compassion,
the ocean took refuge in the lord and worshipped him. / Rāghava, having refilled the ocean again with the missile of Varuṇa,
at the word of the ocean, made a bridge across the ocean, the abode of sea monsters; / Nala caused the bridge to be built with mountains brought by the monkeys.
Then, having gone to the city of Laṅkā and encamped the great army, / a proper battle took place between the monkeys and the rakṣases.
Then the son of the ten-faced one, Śakrajit, a mighty rākṣasa, / bound both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with serpent-nooses.
The son of Vinatā arrived and released those weapons. / The rākṣasas were all struck down by the monkeys of great strength.
The heroic Kumbhakarṇa of great might, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa, / Rāma struck down in battle with arrows resembling flames of fire.
Enraged, Indrajit felled the monkeys with the missile of Brahmā. / By Hanūmat was brought the mountain of great medicinal herbs;
and by the touch of that which had been brought, all of them indeed arose. / Then the heroic younger brother of Rāma, in battle,
felled the conqueror of Śakra with arrows, like the bearer of the thunderbolt [felling] Vṛtra. / Then the descendant of Pulastya marched forth to fight with Rāma in combat,
along with the fourfold forces and ministers, the one of great strength. / An equal battle took place everywhere between the monkeys and the rakṣases,
and between Rāma and Rāvaṇa, and likewise with the son of Sumitrā. / With a spear, the lord of rākṣasas felled Lakṣmaṇa.
Then enraged, Rāghava of great splendor, the destroyer of the rākṣasas, / struck down the heroic rākṣasas with arrows resembling Death at the end of time.
With thousands of blazing arrows greatly resembling the rod of Death, / the descendant of Kakutstha completely covered the rākṣasa with ten necks.
With all his limbs pierced by Rāghava's missiles, / that night-stalker fled from the battlefield to Laṅkā in terror.
Seeing the whole world filled with Rāma, he entered his palace in despondency. / Then the great mountain of potent herbs was brought by Hanūmat.
By it Rāma's younger brother quickly regained consciousness then. / Thereupon the ten-necked one began a sacrifice, desiring victory.
That hostile rite of the enemy was ruined by the monkey chiefs; / and the descendant of Pulastya marched out again to fight with Rāma.
Mounting a divine chariot, accompanied by many rākṣasas, / then Śatamakhu sent a divine chariot equipped with tawny horses,
along with a charioteer, to Rāghava, being wise. / Mounting the chariot brought by Mātali, the best of the Raghus,
praised by the hosts of gods, fought with that demon. / Then a terrible, great battle occurred between Rāma and Rāvaṇa,
lasting seven full days and nights, extremely frightening with weapons and missiles. / All the gods standing in aerial cars watched that encounter there.
The best of the Raghus cut off the heads of the ten-necked one; / but they sprang up repeatedly due to the boon granted by Kapardin.
For the slaying of this wicked soul, Rāghava swiftly released / the Brahmā missile, extremely terrifying, radiant like the fire of destruction.
That missile, discharged by Rāghava, tore through Rāvaṇa's chest, / cleaved the earth, and entered the subterranean realm of Rasātala.
Worshiped by the serpents, it returned to Rāghava's hand. / That great daitya, his life gone, fell and died.
Then all the hosts of gods, their minds overwhelmed with joy, / showered rainfalls of flowers upon the great-souled teacher of the world.
The lords of the gandharvas sang and the hosts of apsarases danced; / auspicious winds blew, and the sun shone with great brilliance.
Sages, siddhas, gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras praised him. / Having consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa, the foremost among the rākṣasas, in Laṅkā,
the best of the Raghu lineage considered himself to have achieved his purpose. / Having consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa, Rāma spoke these words there:
Rāma said: / 'As long as the moon and the sun endure, as long as the earth stands, / and as long as my story is told in the world, so long shall kingship remain with Vibhīṣaṇa.
Going to my divine, eternal abode accessible only to yogins, / attain it, O mighty one, along with your sons, grandsons, and retinue.'
The Lord said: / Having thus granted the boon to that rākṣasa, the mighty one, / having received the daughter of Mithilā there, in the assembly of the people,
Rāghava spoke many harsh and reproaching words to Sītā. / Reproached by him, that virtuous woman entered a great fire.
Then all the hosts of gods, headed by Śiva and Brahmā, / seeing the mother entering the fire, distressed with fear, / approached the best of the Raghus and with joined palms said:
The gods said: / 'O Rāma, Rāma, mighty-armed one, listen, O you of extreme valor! / Sītā is exceedingly pure, virtuous, and by nature never separated from you.
She should not be cast off in vain, just as radiance cannot be cast off by the sun. / She has manifested on the surface of the earth for the welfare of the world,
the mother of the entire universe, the refuge of all the world. / Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa were your former devoted servants.
Due to the curse of Sanaka and the others, they were born on the surface of the earth. / Only for their liberation was Vaidehī seized in the Daṇḍaka forest.
Both of those foremost rākṣasas have indeed been slain by you. / Liberated, they have gone to heaven, accompanied by their sons, grandsons, and followers.
You are Viṣṇu; you are the supreme Brahman, eternal, to be meditated upon by yogins. / You alone are the beginningless, endless, imperishable source of all gods.
You are indeed glorious Nārāyaṇa; Sītā is eternal Lakṣmī. / She is the mother of all worlds; you are the father, the Supreme Lord.
She is the eternal mother of the universe, never separated from you. / Just as you are all-pervading, so too is she, O best of the Raghus.
Therefore accept Sītā, of pure conduct, virtuous and firm in her vows, / without delay, gentle descendant of Kakutstha, like [Lakṣmī] from the ocean of milk!'

The Lord said: / In the meantime, Fire himself, the witness of the world, / taking Sītā, presented her to Rāma in the presence of the gods. / Fire, who dwells within the bodies of all, said to the descendant of Kakutstha there:
Fire said: / 'This Sītā is of pure conduct and stainless, O lord! / Accept her without delay, O Rāma; I speak the truth, the truth to you.'
The Lord said: / Then, at the word of Fire, taking Sītā back, the bearer of the Raghu lineage, / Rāma, became overjoyed, being worshiped by the foremost of the gods.
Those foremost monkeys who had been slain by the rākṣasas in the battle, / by the boon of the Grandfather, quickly arose alive.
Then the lord of the rākṣasas [gave] the aerial car named Puṣpaka, radiant like the sun, / which had belonged to Kubera and had been seized in battle by his brother.
He gave it to Rāghava, along with garments and ornaments. / Honored by him, glorious, powerful Rāmacandra
mounted the excellent aerial car together with his wife Vaidehī / and with his valiant brother Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Daśaratha;
with hosts of bears and monkeys, with the great-souled Sugrīva, / with the valiant Vibhīṣaṇa, and with the mighty rākṣasas.
Just as in the aerial car in Vaikuṇṭha with the great souls who are eternally liberated, / so too all the bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas mounted it.
Praised by the foremost of gods, Rāma departed for Ayodhyā. / Having reached the hermitage of Bharadvāja, Rāma of true valor
dispatched Hanūmat to the presence of Bharata. / Going to the dwelling of the Niṣādas and seeing Guha, the devotee of Viṣṇu,
the foremost monkey announced Rāghava's arrival to him. / Then going to Nandigrāma and seeing that younger brother of Rāghava,
he likewise reported to him the festive arrival of Rāma. / And Bharata, hearing from the monkey that the best of the Raghus had arrived,
experienced incomparable delight along with his younger brother and his friends. / Returning to the descendant of Kakutstha, Hanūmān, the son of the Wind,
reported all the news of Bharata to Rāma. / But descending from the excellent aerial car with his younger brother,
Rāghava, together with his wife, paid homage to the son of Bharadvāja, that store of ascetic power. / And that sage honored the descendant of Kakutstha along with his younger brother
with cooked food, fruits, roots, garments, and ornaments. / Honored by him there and bowing down to that best of sages,
permitted [to depart], Rāma, along with his followers, mounted Puṣpaka then / and went to Nandigrāma by Puṣpaka, surrounded by his friends.
With ministers, leading citizens, his younger brother, / and excellent kings with their armies, the son of Kaikeyī joyfully went out to meet his elder brother.
Reaching the tiger among the Raghus, he bowed down, surrounded by his followers. / Then descending from Puṣpaka, Rāghava, the tormentor of his foes,
approached and embraced Bharata and Śatrughna. / And to the family priest Vasiṣṭha, his elders, his mothers, and his kinsmen,
the immensely radiant one bowed along with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa. / And Vibhīṣaṇa, Sugrīva, Jāmbavat, and Aṅgada,
Hanūmat, and Suṣeṇa, Bharata embraced, / along with his brothers and followers there, following an auspicious bath.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine fragrant unguents, / he mounted the auspicious, celestial chariot driven by Sumantra.
Praised by the gods, along with Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa, / and also Bharata, Sugrīva, Śatrughna, and Vibhīṣaṇa,
Aṅgada, Suṣeṇa, Jāmbavān, the son of the wind-god [Hanumān], / Nīla, the fortunate Nala, Śarabha, and Gandhamādana,
and other heroic monkeys, Guha the lord of the Niṣādas, / rākṣasas of great valor, and mighty sovereigns,

having fully mounted their auspicious elephants and horses in great numbers, / with varied auspicious musical instruments and abundant hymns of praise,

surrounded by bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas, and the excellent soldiers of the Niṣādas, / he of great splendor entered the imperishable city of Sāketa.

Beholding the royal city on the path, the prince, meditating on the king his father alone, / Rāma entered the palace that was purified by the pacing of the sacred feet of Sugrīva, Māruti, and Vibhīṣaṇa.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-second chapter, named 'Rāma's Entry into Ayodhyā,' in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand [verses].

6.243.m: Śaṅkara said: / Then, on that sacred day, at an auspicious and fortunate moment, / the people performed the auspicious rites for the sake of the auspicious consecration.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, and also Kaśyapa, / Mārkaṇḍeya, Maudgalya, Parvata, and Nārada—
these great sages, having preceded [the rite] with recitation and burnt offerings, / those ascetics performed the auspicious consecration of the best of kings.
Having seated [him] together with Sītā on a celestial golden throne set with various jewels and endowed with auspiciousness, / like Janārdana with Śrī,
with divine golden pitchers adorned with various gems and auspicious, / filled with the sacred waters of all pilgrimage sites together with auspicious articles,
endowed with the tips of dūrvā grass, tulasī leaves, flowers, and scents, / with pure waters sanctified by mantras, the ascetics of resolute vows,
chanting the auspicious hymns to Viṣṇu that consist of the four Vedas, / performed the auspicious consecration of the descendant of Kakutstha, the lord of the world.
At that most auspicious astrological moment, divine drums resounded in heaven, / and showers of flowers fell on all sides.
With divine garments and ornaments, and divine fragrant unguents, / and with various kinds of celestial flowers, the descendant of Raghu together with his queen
was adorned by the sages who had mastered the Vedas and shone resplendently. / Lakṣmaṇa then held the divine parasol and chowrie;
at his side, Bharata and Śatrughna shone wielding palm-leaf fans; / the glorious Vibhīṣaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, presented a mirror;
Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, held the full jar; / and Jāmbavān, of great splendor, held a charming garland of flowers;
the son of Vālin [Aṅgada] offered betel with camphor to Hari; / Hanumān held the celestial lamp, and Suṣeṇa the auspicious banner.
Surrounding the great-souled one, the ministers attended upon him: / Sṛṣṭi, Jayanta, Vijaya, Saurāṣṭra, Rāṣṭravardhana,
Akopa, Dharmapāla, and Sumantra are traditionally known as the ministers. / And the kings, tigers among men, rulers of various realms,
citizens, and elders of trade guilds attended upon the king. / Surrounded by bears, monkey chiefs, ministers, lords of the earth,
rākṣasas, eminent twice-born men, and attendants— / just as the husband of Kamalā [Viṣṇu], dwelling in the highest heaven, is surrounded by deities—
even so the glorious best of kings shone then in Sāketa: / dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with eyes resembling lotus leaves,
with arms reaching to his knees, Kakutstha's descendant, Hari wearing yellow garments, / with a conch-like neck, a broad chest, adorned with varied ornaments.
Beholding the best of the Raghus seated together with his queen, consecrated, / the hosts of gods standing on their celestial chariots, their minds filled with joy,
and the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases praised him with shouts of victory. / Then, consecrated by the great sages headed by Vasiṣṭha,
Rāma shone with Queen Sītā like Nārāyaṇa with Śrī. / Afraid because of his superhuman nature, [yet eager] to worship his lotus feet,

Śaṅkara, having approached in delight, seeing [him], praised him with a joyous soul; / having folded his hands in reverence, filled with bliss and stammering with emotion, / delighting all the gods, sages, and monkeys.
Mahādeva said: / Homage to the primal material nature, eternal, to the supreme Self, / whose form is being, consciousness, and bliss, who has the universe as his form, the creator!
Homage to Viṣṇu, the root and bulb of uninterrupted bliss, / whose form grants bliss to the three worlds, whose form is divine!
Homage to him who is worshiped by Brahmā and Indra, who grants fearlessness to Śaṅkara! / Homage to the one whose essential nature is Viṣṇu; homage, homage to you whose form is all!
To the creator of origin, maintenance, and destruction, the soul of the three guṇas, / homage be to the great-souled one whose essential nature is free of limiting adjuncts!
To him who assumes limiting adjuncts by means of this divine Vidyā, Sītā! / Homage to the two of you, Spirit and Matter, for the sake of the worlds,
to the mother and father of the universe, to the Mother and to Rāghava! / Homage to her whose form is phenomenal reality, and to him whose form is free from phenomenal reality!

Homage to her whose form is meditation, and to the embodiment of the Self who is the object of yogis' meditation! / Homage, homage to the two of you who are devoid of transformation and non-transformation!
To Sītā, who is the unchanging seed, and to Rāghava! / Sītā is Lakṣmī, you are Viṣṇu; Sītā is Gaurī, you are Śiva;
Sītā herself is Sāvitrī, and you are the four-faced Brahmā; / Sītā is Śacī, you are Śakra; Sītā is Svāhā, you are the fire;
Sītā is the destroying goddess, and you assume the form of Yama; / Sītā is indeed all prosperity, and you are Kubera, O best of the Raghus;
Sītā is the goddess Rudrāṇī, and you are the mighty Rudra; / Sītā is the goddess Rohiṇī, and you are the moon, bestower of happiness on the worlds;
Sītā is Saṃjñā, you are the sun; Sītā is the night, you are the day; / Sītā is the goddess Mahākālī, and you are ever Mahākāla.
Whatever in the three worlds has the feminine gender, that is entirely Jānakī; / whatever is marked by a masculine name, that indeed is all you, O Lord!
Everywhere, O Lord of all the gods, Sītā is the bearer everywhere; / then you too are [there] to protect; her power sustains the universe.
Therefore, the merit marked out by the two of you is multiplied ten-millionfold; / your life story, marked by Śiva and Śakti, bestows peace.
We two, Rāma, worship the world; Umā and I are ever worshipers of you two: / Gaurī mutters your name, and I am a reciter of your mantra.
To one who is about to die at Maṇikarṇikā, residing half in the water, / I impart your saving mantra, which bestows Brahman.
Therefore, O Lord of Jānakī, you are certainly the Supreme Brahman! / Deluded by your māyā, all do not know you in truth.
The Lord said: / Addressed thus by Śambhu, Rāma became inclined to grant favor, / assuming a divine form, glorious, wondrous to behold.
Then, beholding that form, men, monkeys, and gods / were not able even to look upon that great and wondrous brilliance.

Out of awe, the foremost of the gods bowed down with intense devotion. / And realizing that the men, monkeys, and gods were terrified, Rāma / assumed the state of an illusory human and addressed the gods once more:

Rāmacandra said:
"Listen, deities: whoever praises me every day
with the hymn spoken by Śambhu, that man will become equal to a god.

Freed from all sins, he attains my own nature.
He gains victory in battle, and is never thwarted anywhere.

He is not troubled by ghosts, vetālas, malevolent rites, or astrological planets.
A sonless man obtains a son, and a maiden finds a husband.

A poor man attains wealth, and becomes virtuous and disciplined of character.
He is born possessing might equal to my own, endowed with fortune; there is no doubt about this.

There is freedom from obstacles for men in all undertakings and all ventures.
Whatever desire—even a wish exceedingly difficult to attain—a mortal longs for,

he achieves success within six months by the grace of this hymn.
Whatever merit lies in all sacred fords, whatever reward in all sacrifices—
that reward is obtained ten million times over through this hymn."

The Lord [Śiva] said:
Having spoken thus, that Rāmacandra dismissed Maheśvara,
and dismissed all the gods who had arrived, headed by Brahmā.

All men, monkeys, and deities were honored,
and dismissed by Rāmacandra, filled with the utmost love.

Thus dismissed, indeed all of them departed in joy, exceedingly delighted,
reciting the supreme hymn uttered by the Lord [Śiva] and remembering Rāma, whose form is the universe, the best of boons.
